paper_metadata.title: Effect of Fe additions on the microstructure and properties of Nb-Mo-Ti alloys
paper_metadata.journal: International Journal of Refractory Metals & Hard Materials

evidence.quote: Effect of Fe additions on the microstructure and properties of Nb-Mo-Ti alloys

According to X-ray diffraction, the studied alloys have single-phase BCC structures (Fig. 1).

SEM analysis confirms single-phase, equiaxed grain structures for the alloys (Fig. 2). The average grain size in M2 and M3 alloys is 0.90 mm and 0.60 mm, respectively (Fig. 2a,b). The average grain size in the Fe-containing alloys M2Fe and M3Fe is 0.44 mm and 0.39 mm, respectively (Fig. 2c,d).
Small dark spots inside grains are pores and/or nitride particles rich in Ti.

In the M3 alloy these clusters are almost always separated from grain boundaries by a thin (~2–3 μm) precipitation-free zone (Fig. 4c). Thinner (up to 1 μm) precipitation-free zones are also observed near some GBs in the annealed M3Fe alloy;

attributes.morphology: irregular shapes at GBs, needle-like near GBs

evidence.quote: In addition, precipitation of Ti rich (50–68 at.%Ti) particles near and at grain boundaries (GBs) occurs in the annealed samples (Figs. 4c,d). The GB particles have irregular shapes, while the precipitates near GBs have needle-like appearance and are arranged in ~10–15 μm thickness/diameter clusters."

These small additions of Fe did not form secondary phases but noticeably increased the strength of the Nb-Mo-Ti alloys in the temperature range of 25 to 1200°C due to solid solution strengthening effect.

Assuming a superposition between the classical thermally activated strengthening (modeled here using the Suzuki model) and short range order strengthening, the expected strengthening due to Fe in M3Fe alloy is calculated to be 235–256 MPa at room temperature and 186–193 MPa at 1000°C.
